20250318_7483146603738483990.description: Navigating at night? Understanding anchor lights is essential for safety! ⚓️ We break down the differences between vessels over and under 50 meters. Learn why larger vessels display two lights (fore and aft) and smaller ones just one. Stay safe on the water! #MaritimeSafety #NavigationLights #AnchoredVessel #BoatingSafety #SailingTips #MarineRegulations #nightnavigation #CapCut
20250318_7483146603738483990.transcript: The open sea at night can be a beautiful, but potentially dangerous place. Visibility is limited, and ensuring the safety of all vessels is paramount. When a vessel comes to anchor, it's essential to signal its presence to other ships. The rules for this are clear and designed to prevent collisions. For smaller vessels, under 50 meters, the requirement is: A single, all-round white light, positioned where it can be best seen, is all that's needed. This light must be visible from every direction, ensuring it can be spotted by approaching vessels. It must be visible for at least two nautical miles. This light serves as a clear indication that the vessel is at anchor and not underway. But what about larger vessels? Those over 50 meters in length have a different lighting requirement. These vessels must display two all-round white lights. One is placed at the fore, or forward part of the ship, and the other at or near the stern, the rear. The stern light must be positioned at a lower level than the forward light. This difference in height helps other vessels determine the size and orientation of the anchored ship. Both lights must be visible for at least three nautical miles. Vessels over 100 meters must also illuminate their decks to enhance visibility. So, the next time you see a light on the water at night, remember the important role it plays in keeping everyone safe.
20250318_7483146603738483990.summary: Explains the anchor light requirements for vessels under and over 50 meters length under COLREGs.

20250318_7483149317268638978.description: Mastering night navigation! 💡 We're diving into the specific navigation lights displayed by vessels over 50 meters when underway. Discover the mandatory sidelights, masthead lights, and stern light, and understand their significance in preventing collisions. #NavigationRules #MaritimeLaw #ShipLights #SailingTips #OceanNavigation #BoatSafety #NauticalKnowledge #MarineLife  #CapCut
20250318_7483149317268638978.transcript: A vessel over 50 meters making way at night must display specific navigation lights. A forward masthead light visible for six nautical miles. A second after masthead light positioned higher and also visible for six nautical miles. Two sidelights: red for port, green for starboard, both visible for three nautical miles. Finally, a stern light visible for three nautical miles. These lights ensure the vessel's presence and direction are clearly visible to other nearby vessels. When approaching a ship from its port side, you will see two white lights and the red port side light. When approaching a ship from the starboard side, you will see two white lights and green starboard side light. When following a ship, you will see a single white light. Finally, if it's dead ahead, then you will see all forward-facing lights, but be sure to alter your course to starboard as this indicates you're on a course for collision.
20250318_7483149317268638978.summary: Explains the navigation light configuration and visibility ranges for power-driven vessels over 50 meters underway at night, and how to identify their aspect.

20250319_7483479165237218582.transcript: Lost control of your vessel at night, but still moving through the water? You're not under command. This means your vessel is underway, but due to uncontrollable circumstances, you cannot comply with the collision regulations. So, what now? Display two red lights vertically. This signals to other vessels that you are not under command. Since you are still making way through the water, you must also show your standard navigation lights, including sidelights and a stern light. Remember: Red over red, my steering is dead. If you see a vessel displaying these lights, stay well clear of them and their intended course. If you see a vessel without its sidelights, this could also mean that the vessel is aground and unable to maneuver. Finally, even though your vessel is not under command, it is vital to ensure you still keep a lookout and ensure you are able to communicate with other vessels. Stay safe at sea.
20250319_7483479165237218582.summary: A vessel that is Not Under Command (NUC) and making way through the water at night must display two all-round red lights vertically along with its sidelights and stern light.

20250319_7483523128749051158.transcript: Engaged in operations that limit your ability to manoeuvre? You're restricted in ability to manoeuvre. You must give way to a vessel that is restricted in ability to manoeuvre, and it should be treated as the stand-on vessel.

20250325_7485719213840010518.transcript: Navigating near dredging or underwater operations at night. Understanding their light signals is vital for safety. Vessels involved in dredging and underwater operations fall under Rule 27. These vessels display a vertical line of red, white, red all-round lights, indicating they are restricted in their ability to manoeuvre. To indicate the safe passage side, they display two vertical all-round green lights on the side where passage is clear. Conversely, two vertical all-round red lights indicate the obstructed side, where passage is unsafe. If the vessel is at anchor, it must follow the lights prescribed in Rule 27, not Rule 30. When making headway, the vessel must also display its standard navigation lights, including side lights and a stern light. Stay safe at sea.
20250325_7485719213840010518.summary: Vessels engaged in dredging or underwater operations display red-white-red lights for restricted manoeuvrability, green lights for clear passage, red lights for obstructed side, and standard navigation lights when making headway.

20250330_7487603693819333910.transcript: You're traveling through open water when you see a vessel coming straight towards you. So, what's next? Rule 14 of the International Collision Regulations states that when two power-driven vessels are meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses creating a risk of collision, each shall alter its course to starboard so that they pass port side to port side. If you ever in doubt about whether a collision risk exists, assume there is one and take action accordingly. It's always safer to adjust your course than to wait too long. Staying alert and proactive is key to avoiding collisions. Stay safe at sea.
20250330_7487603693819333910.summary: Under COLREG Rule 14, when two power-driven vessels meet head-on, both must alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port.

20250411_7492030103619177750.transcript: In an emergency at sea, being found quickly is critical. That's where your Search and Rescue Transponder comes in. Learn how to act safely and avoid incidents at sea. #COLREGs #Rule15 #MaritimeSafety #NavigationRules #Boating #Sailing #SeaSafety #LearnOnTikTok #UKBoating #USBoating #BoatSmart #BoatingTips #Navigation #RulesOfTheRoad #GiveWayVessel
20250508_7501965970961976598.transcript: In a crossing situation, two vessels are approaching each other at an angle, creating a risk of collision. Rule 15 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea dictates which vessel must give way. The vessel which has the other on its starboard side is the give-way vessel. In this scenario, vessel A has vessel B on its starboard side. Therefore, vessel A is the give-way vessel. The give-way vessel, vessel A, must take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the other vessel. The most common action is to alter course to starboard, passing astern of vessel B. Vessel B is the stand-on vessel. It must maintain its course and speed. However, if it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, the stand-on vessel may take action to avoid collision. Remember, in a crossing situation, the vessel with the other on its starboard side must give way. Early and decisive action is crucial to prevent collisions and ensure safety at sea. Stay safe at sea.
20250508_7501965970961976598.summary: Under COLREGs Rule 15 for crossing situations, the vessel with the other on its starboard side must give way early and substantially, typically by altering course to starboard.

20250613_7515420855942384918.description: When you're on the water, Rule 13 of the COLREGS is non-negotiable! This rule on overtaking is crystal clear: if you're coming up on another vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft their beam (basically, from behind their widest point), you are the overtaking vessel, and you MUST keep clear. 20260318_7618519783184551190.transcript: A vessel over 50 meters making way at night must display specific navigation lights. A forward masthead light visible for 6 nautical miles. A second after masthead light positioned higher and also visible for 6 nautical miles. Two sidelights: red for port, green for starboard, both visible for 3 nautical miles. Finally, a stern light visible for 3 nautical miles. These lights ensure the vessel's presence and direction are clearly visible to other nearby vessels. When approaching a ship from its port side, you will see two white lights and the red port side light. When approaching a ship from the starboard side, you will see two white lights and green starboard side light. When following a ship, you will see a single white light. Finally, if it's dead ahead, then you will see all forward-facing lights, but be sure to alter your course to starboard as this indicates you're on a course for collision.

20260318_7618520537022598402.transcript: The open sea at night can be a beautiful, but potentially dangerous place. Visibility is limited, and ensuring the safety of all vessels is paramount. When a vessel comes to anchor, it's essential to signal its presence to other ships. The rules for this are clear and designed to prevent collisions. For smaller vessels, under 50 meters, the requirement is: a single, all-round white light, positioned where it can be best seen, is all that's needed. This light must be visible from every direction, ensuring it can be spotted by approaching vessels. It must be visible for at least two nautical miles. This light serves as a clear indication that the vessel is at anchor and not underway. But what about larger vessels? Those over 50 meters in length have a different lighting requirement. These vessels must display two all-round white lights. One is placed at the fore, or forward part of the ship, and the other at or near the stern, the rear. The stern light must be positioned at a lower level than the forward light. This difference in height helps other vessels determine the size and orientation of the anchored ship. Both lights must be visible for at least three nautical miles. Vessels over 100 meters must also illuminate their decks to enhance visibility. So, the next time you see a light on the water at night, remember the important role it plays in keeping everyone safe.

20260714_7662148471243148566.transcript: This skipper is about to run aground, and the cause is a single number he never checked. A vessel's draft, also spelled draught, is the vertical distance from the waterline straight down to the lowest point of the keel. You read the draft from marks painted near the bow and stern on both sides, with some vessels also carrying marks amidships. Each metric figure is 10 cm tall with a 10 cm gap, and marks an even tenth of a meter. So water at the base of a figure reads that exact value, while water at its top reads one tenth of a meter higher. The reading at the bow is your forward draft, and the reading at the stern is your aft draft. Add the forward and aft readings and halve them, and you get the mean draft, a working figure for the average depth of the whole hull. The difference between the forward and aft readings is the trim. So a deeper stern means the boat is trimmed by the stern. Do not confuse draft with air draft, the height from the waterline up to the highest fixed point of the whole vessel, including the antenna and instruments mounted above the masthead. Draft matters because the gap between your keel and the seabed is your under-keel clearance, which must always stay above a set safety margin, not just above zero. Remember that speed makes the hull squat lower in shallow water, and a falling tide steals depth from under you. Know your draft, keep a safe margin of clearance, and plan for tide and squat before you ever leave the dock.

As a slack tank heels, its flat liquid surface stays level and a wedge slides to the low side, causing a virtual rise of G that quietly eats your effective GM, and because the effect scales with breadth cubed, wide shallow water is the real killer, the same failure that took the Herald of Free Enterprise. Press your tanks up, subdivide them, clear water off the deck, and follow along for the next stability lesson. #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #maritimetraining #learnontiktok #maritimemaster #deckcadet #sailing #boating #navigation #seafarer⚓️
20260714_7662392405559168278.transcript: A half full tank is more dangerous than a full one, and loose water has capsized ships. The ghost G that shaved our GM hides in the level top of a slack tank, the free surface. When she heels, the surface stays level, so a wedge of liquid slides to the low side. That shift drags G toward the low side, expressed as a virtual rise of G that eats effective GM. The surprise is that this loss barely depends on how much liquid is aboard, and the breadth of that surface dominates because its effect is cubed. A wide shallow spread is worse than a narrow deep one of equal volume, because doubling breadth is eight times worse. A full or empty tank has no free surface, but a slack one does, so correct GM below about 98% full. This is why we subdivide, because one bulkhead cuts the effect to a quarter, and a second to a ninth. The worst case is water on an undivided car deck, which capsized the Herald of Free Enterprise in about 90 seconds. That is why ferries now confirm the bow doors are shut with bridge indicator lights and monitoring, and follow far stricter damage stability rules. So any wide free surface is your enemy: press tanks up, subdivide, clear water off deck, and follow for more.
20260714_7662392405559168278.summary: Free surface effect in slack tanks causes a virtual rise in center of gravity and reduces GM, scaling exponentially with the breadth of the liquid surface.

20260715_7662710914327514390.description: In fog, who is the stand on vessel? Trick question. Nobody is. The moment two vessels cannot see each other in or near restricted visibility, COLREGs Rule 19 takes over and Rules 11 to 18 switch off. There is no stand on and no give way, so both vessels must act to keep clear. What Rule 19 actually demands: 🌫️ A safe speed for the conditions, engines ready for immediate manoeuvre (19b, tied to Rule 6) 📡 Detect a contact by radar alone, judge if close quarters or risk of collision is developing, then take avoiding action in ample time (19d) ↩️ Forward of the beam, so far as possible never alter to port (unless you are overtaking) ↪️ Abeam or abaft the beam, so far as possible never alter toward her 🔊 Hear a fog signal apparently forward of your beam and you cannot rule out collision? Slow to bare steerageway, take all way off if you must, and navigate with extreme caution (19e) In fog nobody stands on, everybody slows down, everybody keeps clear. Save this before your next foggy passage and follow for more Rule of the Road. #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #maritimetraining #learnontiktok #maritimemaster #deckcadet #boating #navigation #seafarer⚓️ #colregs #rule19
20260715_7662710914327514390.transcript: Zero visibility, a radar contact closing in, and you cannot see it. So which of you stands on, and which way do you turn? The moment two vessels are not in sight of one another, in or near fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rainstorms, sandstorms, or any other similar causes, you are in Rule 19. Because you cannot see each other, Rules 11 to 18 do not apply, so there is no stand-on and no give-way, and both of you must act to keep clear. Rule 19b demands a safe speed for the conditions, and power-driven vessels must keep their engines ready for immediate manoeuvre. Learn your beam sectors, because a contact is forward of the beam under 90 degrees from ahead, abeam at about 90, or abaft the beam beyond 90. Detect another vessel by radar alone, and you must judge whether close quarters or risk of collision is developing, then take avoiding action in ample time. For a target forward of the beam, so far as possible never alter to port, the only exception being a vessel you are overtaking, so you normally turn to starboard. But for a vessel abeam or abaft the beam, the word changes to toward, so far as possible never alter course toward her. Unless you have ruled out risk of collision, a fog signal apparently forward of your beam means slow to the minimum that holds your course, take all way off if you must, and navigate with extreme caution. In fog, nobody stands on, everybody slows, everybody keeps clear, because it is Rule 19. So master your radar, CPA and TCPA, and follow for more Rule of the Road.
20260715_7662710914327514390.summary: In restricted visibility, COLREGs Rule 19 applies, removing stand-on/give-way obligations so both vessels must reduce speed and take avoiding action based on radar and sound signals.

20260716_7662150830971358487.description: Your ship sinks deeper the faster she goes, and cargo has nothing to do with it. That is squat, and this one covers why it happens, when it starts to bite, and the quick Barrass sum that tells you how much clearance you are losing. Watch to the end, then save it for your next shallow water passage.  #underkeelclearance #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #boating #maritime #learnontiktok #maritimemaster #deckcadet
20260716_7662150830971358487.transcript: Watch the gap under this keel vanish. She is not overloaded, she is sinking just by moving fast in shallow water. That is squat: sinkage plus a trim change while she moves, fading as her speed through the water dies to zero. Static draft plus squat gives your dynamic draft, and whatever water is left below the keel is your underkeel clearance. Water squeezed under the hull speeds up, and Bernoulli says faster flow means lower pressure, sucking her body deeper. Squat grows with speed squared, so double your speed and you get roughly four times the squat. Squat starts to bite once depth falls below about twice your draft, and gets serious under 1.5. Squeeze into a confined channel and the banks trap that fast flow, roughly doubling your squat compared with open water. Full-form hulls, block coefficient above 0.7, squat by the bow, while fine-form hulls squat by the stern. Quick Barrass estimate: squat in meters equals block coefficient times speed through the water in knots squared over 100 in open water, or 50 in a confined channel. Our bulker at 10 knots through the water in a channel, 0.8 times 100 divided by 50 is 1.6 meters of squat. Squat silently eats your clearance, so plan for it. And remember, half speed means quarter squat.
20260716_7662150830971358487.summary: Learn how vessel speed, depth-to-draft ratio, hull shape, and channel confinement cause squat, reducing underkeel clearance, and how to estimate it using the Barrass formula.

20260716_7663095862305885462.description: A drifting ship, a dredger, a trawler, a yacht and a motorboat all meet at one point. 20260716_7663095862305885462.transcript: A drifting ship, a dredger, a trawler, a yacht, and a motorboat converge on one point. So who gives way to whom? Rule 18 opens except where Rules 9, 10, and 13 otherwise require, so narrow channels, traffic separation schemes, and overtaking override the whole ladder. A power-driven vessel underway takes the bottom rung, keeping out of the way of not under command, restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, fishing, and sail. One rung up, a sailing vessel underway keeps clear of the three above her: not under command, restricted, and fishing. A vessel engaged in fishing keeps clear of the two on top, but only so far as possible, the rule's own words. Restricted in her ability to manoeuvre shows ball, diamond, ball. Her work, like dredging or laying cable, stops her getting out of your way. Beside her sits not under command, two black balls, unable to keep clear through some exceptional circumstance like a steering failure, and no rule ranks these two. Constrained by her draft is not a rung. All but the top two, if circumstances admit, avoid impeding her safe passage, and she navigates with particular caution. Sailors remember "No Reels Catch Fish, So Purchase Some", and the US inland rules simply drop the C; they have no constrained by draft. Rule 18 only applies between vessels in sight of one another, and it is never a license to hold your course blindly. The less able she is to keep clear, the higher she sits. So know your rung and follow for more rules of the road.
20260716_7663095862305885462.summary: Rule 18 establishes the hierarchy of give-way responsibilities between vessels based on their manoeuvrability.

20260716_7663247528988642582.transcript: Sheet in! Ease the kicker! And in the next minute, every shout on this boat will make sense. The mast is the tall spar, the boom joins it at the gooseneck, and spreaders hold the sidewires wide. Standing rigging holds the mast up: forestay to the bow, backstay to the stern, shrouds each side. Front edge luff, back edge leech stiffened by battens, bottom edge foot, and telltales off the leech show the airflow. 20260717_7662150223283653910.description: That mast is about to hit the bridge, and the skipper thinks there is room to spare. Air draft is the height from your waterline to your highest fixed point, and it changes with cargo and trim while the water level changes your clearance. Watch the full breakdown and save it for your next bridge or overhead cable. #buoyage #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #boating #maritime #learnontiktok #maritimemaster #deckcadet
20260717_7662150223283653910.transcript: That mast is about to hit the bridge, and the skipper still thinks there is room to spare. Air draft is the distance from the waterline straight up to your vessel's highest fixed point. That highest point is often not the masthead itself, so count every antenna, light, and instrument fixed above it. If a component folds down, fold it down, because anything left standing counts towards your air draft. Draft mirrors it down to the keel, and loading cargo sits her deeper, so the draft grows and the air draft shrinks. Unload and it reverses, and trim tilts your highest point, too, so air draft is never one fixed number. Under a fixed bridge, the water level moves, too, and at high water, there is less clearance overhead. Charts print a vertical clearance for bridges, cables, and overhead pipes above a stated water level, so check which level your chart uses. Overhead power cables can arc before you ever touch them, so use the safe clearance where charted, and always keep extra margin. Work out today's clearance from the charted figure and the water level, subtract your air draft, and keep a positive margin. Know your air draft before every bridge, cable, or overhead pipe, then catch our boat draft video next.
20260717_7662150223283653910.summary: Air draft is the height from the waterline to the vessel's highest fixed point, which varies with cargo, trim, and tide, determining safe clearance under bridges and power cables.

20260718_7662151617227083030.transcript: One draft reading is never enough, because a ship almost never floats perfectly level. The forward draft is read where the waterline cuts the draft marks painted on both sides of the bow. The aft draft is the matching reading at the stern marks, and here the stern floats deeper. Add the forward draft to the aft draft and divide the total by two, and that average is your mean draft. 6.0 forward plus 7.0 aft makes 13, and half of 13 gives a mean draft of 6.5 m. That single figure checks your ship against its load line limit, and drives the draft surveys that weigh your cargo. Never plan under keel clearance on the mean, because the seabed meets your deepest point. And here, that is the 7 m stern. Long steel hulls hog and sag, so surveyors also read the amidships marks and weight the average toward amidships for the displacement draft. Read the bow, read the stern, halve the sum for your mean draft, and save this one for your next draft survey.
20260718_7662151617227083030.summary: Learn how to calculate a ship's mean draft and why under-keel clearance must be calculated from the deepest draft rather than the mean.

20260719_7662152650045082902.description: That circle with a line through it on the side of nearly every cargo ship is not decoration, it is the law. One Victorian reformer fought to get it there after overloaded coffin ships drowned thousands of sailors, and it still decides how deep a ship may sit today. Watch to the end to decode TF, F, T, S, W and WNA, then save it for the next hull you spot. #boating #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #learnontiktok #maritime #maritimemaster #deckcadet #shipstability
20260719_7662152650045082902.transcript: Why does nearly every cargo ship on earth have a circle with a line through it painted right midships? That is the Plimsoll mark, the deepest this ship may legally sit in saltwater in summer. Victorian reformer Samuel Plimsoll fought to make it law after overloaded coffin ships drowned thousands of sailors in the 1870s. The letters beside the circle name the assigning authority, usually a classification society, and a short deck line sits above. Forward of the circle runs a comb of extra lines marked TF, F, T, S, W, and WNA. They stand for Tropical Fresh, Fresh, Tropical, Summer, Winter, and Winter North Atlantic. Fresh water is less dense than salt water, so the same ship floats deeper, and that is why the fresh lines sit above the circle. The oceans are mapped into seasonal zones, so the line you may load to depends on where and when you sail. Winter North Atlantic sits lowest of all, extra margin for ships of 100 meters or less, crossing that ocean in winter. The gap from waterline to deck line is freeboard, the safety margin that gives the ship reserve buoyancy to rise over every wave. Adopted in 1966, the IMO Load Lines Convention makes that little circle global law, so save this for the next hull you spot.
20260719_7662152650045082902.summary: Learn how the Plimsoll mark and load line markings indicate maximum draft and freeboard across different water densities and seasonal zones.

20260719_7664284540734622998.description: Thick fog, pitch black night, and your radar has already found the ship you cannot see. In under 90 seconds: how radio pulses become range, bearing and a live picture of everything around your vessel, why it works when your eyes fail, and the honest limits every skipper should respect (small GRP boats, sea clutter, rain). COLREGs Rule 7 says use it properly, so save this one for your next night passage. #learnontiktok #maritimetraining #maritimemaster #boating #navigation #deckcadet #sailing #seafarer⚓️ #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️
20260719_7664284540734622998.transcript: Thick fog, pitch black night. A ship out there somewhere, and you cannot see a thing, but your radar already has it. Radar stands for radio detection and ranging, and the name tells you exactly what it does. A rotating aerial called the scanner fires out short pulses of radio energy as it sweeps around the horizon. When a pulse hits something solid, a ship, a buoy, or a coastline, part of it bounces straight back as an echo. Radio waves travel at a known speed, the speed of light, so timing how long the echo takes to come back gives the target's range. And the direction the aerial is pointing when that echo arrives gives the target's bearing. Put range and bearing together for every echo and the display paints a live picture of everything around you with your own vessel at the center. So in fog, in darkness, and even in rain, the screen keeps painting the ships, land, and buoys your eyes cannot find. Radar is an aid with limits, because small wooden or GRP boats and low targets can return weak echoes, and heavy rain or sea clutter can hide real contacts. That is why COLREGs Rule 7 says radar must be used properly if it is fitted and operational, and that you must never make assumptions on scanty radar information. Radar hands you the range and bearing of everything around you, your eyes when you cannot see.
20260719_7664284540734622998.summary: Understand how marine radar measures target range and bearing through radio echoes, and learn its operational limits under COLREGs Rule 7.

20260720_7662153729885408534.description: Three ships, the exact same eight degree lean, but only one of them should scare you. In 75 seconds you will know the difference between heel, list and angle of loll, and why fixing the wrong one can capsize a ship. Save this one for your next stability exam. #boating #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #learnontiktok #maritime #maritimemaster #deckcadet #shipstability
20260720_7662153729885408534.transcript: Three ships, the exact same eight degree lean, but only one of them should scare you. Ship one is heeling, pushed over by an outside force such as wind, waves, or a hard turn. Take the force away, and she swings straight back upright. Heel is temporary, and her stability is healthy. Ship two has a list, a steady lean from weight inside her, uneven cargo, ballast, or flooding. While her stability is still positive, the fix is simple: move weight across and she comes back level. Ship three cannot even sit upright. She flops to an angle and hangs there, and that is angle of loll. It happens when her initial GM, the metacentric height, goes negative, so floating upright is no longer stable. The trap is that loll looks exactly like a list, but ballast the high side and she can flop across and capsize. Instead, you put weight down low, filling the divided double bottom tank on the low side first, even though she briefly leans further. Once that tank is pressed full, the low weight restores her stability, and filling the high side then brings her gently upright. Heel passes, list means move weight, loll means lower G first, and next time we unpack the number behind it all.
20260720_7662153729885408534.summary: Understand the crucial distinctions between heel, list, and angle of loll, including why angle of loll is caused by a negative initial metacentric height (GM) and how to safely correct it without capsizing.

20260721_7662158343246499094.description: One number decides whether a ship snaps back upright or flops over and hangs at a lean. GM, the metacentric height, explained in 75 seconds, from G and B to stiff versus tender, angle of loll, and the sneaky free surface effect. Save this one for your stability revision. #boating #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #learnontiktok #maritime #maritimemaster #deckcadet #shipstability #sailing #metacentricheight
20260721_7662158343246499094.transcript: That ship that flopped over and hung there last time, this is the number behind it: GM, the metacentric height. Point 1 is G, her center of gravity, the single balance point of every ton on board. Point 2 is B, the center of buoyancy, sitting at the middle of the underwater volume that holds her up. Heel her over a few degrees, and the underwater shape changes, so B slides toward the low side while G stays put. Draw the buoyancy force straight up through that new B, and where it crosses the center line sits M, the metacenter. GM is the vertical distance from G up to M, and its sign and size set her stability over those first few degrees. Big GM means a stiff ship with a fast, snappy roll, small GM means a tender ship with a slow, lazy roll. Let G climb above M, and GM goes negative, she cannot stay upright, and that steady lean to either side is your angle of loll. In real life, G creeps up, lifted by deck cargo stacked high and by fuel burned off from the double bottoms down low. Slack tanks are sneakier. Their sloshing free surface causes a virtual rise of G that quietly shaves your GM. So GM, big is stiff, small is tender, negative is loll, aim for the middle.
20260721_7662158343246499094.summary: Learners will understand how metacentric height (GM) determines ship stability, distinguishing between stiff and tender movement, angle of loll, and the impacts of free surface effect.

20260722_7662158767018085654.description: Two black balls in a vertical line, do you know what that ship is telling you? Ball, cone, cylinder and diamond, every COLREGs day shape from anchor to a tow over 200 metres, decoded in 72 seconds. Watch to the end and save the recap card to quiz yourself on watch. #colregs #boating #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #learnontiktok #maritimemaster #maritime #deckcadet #shipstability #sailing #seafarer⚓️
20260722_7662158767018085654.transcript: Quick quiz. A ship ahead hoists two black balls in a vertical line, so what is she telling you? She is not under command (Rule 27), and those balls are day shapes, the daytime equivalent of her red over red night lights. The rules build these signals from just four black shapes sized by Annex 1: the ball, the cone, the cylinder, and the diamond. One ball hoisted in the forepart means the vessel is at anchor, and that is Rule 30. Count the balls hoisted where they can best be seen: one means at anchor, two mean not under command, and three in a vertical line mean she is aground. Ball, diamond, ball means restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (Rule 27). Think dredgers, cable layers, and dive support vessels. A vessel constrained by her draught, severely restricted in deviating from her course, may hoist a single black cylinder, the only optional day shape (Rule 28). A cone with the apex pointing down hoisted forward means a sailing vessel that is also motoring (Rule 25). Two cones with their apexes together mean she is engaged in fishing or trawling (Rule 26). When the tow measures over 200 metres from the tug's stern to the tail of the tow, both the tug and the tow hoist a diamond (Rule 24). 20260723_7662159902420389142.transcript: Shout left on a boat and you can send your crewmate to completely the wrong side of the ship. Face the bow, the pointed front end, and the boat's left side is port, its right side is starboard. Turn around and your left and right swap over, but port and starboard stay bolted to the boat. Starboard began as steorbord, the steering side, because early ships hung their steering oar on the right. Crews tied the other side against the wharf to protect that oar, so the harbour side became known as the port side. At night, a vessel underway shows a red light on her port side and a green light to starboard, the same rule all over the world. A ship coming straight at you shows her red port light on your right because the words belong to the ship, not to you. Two tricks to lock it in: port and left both have four letters, and port wine is red, so think red port left. Quiz time. It is night. You spot a single green sidelight out there, so which side of that ship are you looking at? If you said starboard, spot on. A green sidelight means you are looking at her right-hand side. Facing the bow, it is always port, left, and red; starboard, right, and green. So save this for your first day on the water.
20260723_7662159902420389142.summary: Learners will understand the definitions, etymologies, memory tricks, and night sidelight color conventions for port and starboard.

20260724_7662161761583353110.description: The chart says steer 090, the compass says 096, and neither one is lying. In 70 seconds the TVMDC ladder shows how variation and deviation turn a true course into a compass course, worked both ways with real numbers. Save this for your next passage plan.  #navigation #tvmdc #compasserror #boating #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #maritimemaster #learnontiktok #deckcadet
20260724_7662161761583353110.transcript: The chart says steer 090, the compass in front of you says 096, and neither one is lying. True north is chart north, straight up the meridians to the geographic pole, and it is the number you plot. The needle actually follows magnetic north, and the gap from true is called variation, printed on the chart's compass rose. Your own steel and electronics bend the needle further, an extra error called deviation, read from your boat's deviation card. Stack it all on one ladder: True, Variation, Magnetic, Deviation, Compass; TVMDC. Going down the ladder from chart to helm, you add westerly errors and subtract easterly ones. True 090 plus 4 West variation makes 094 magnetic, plus 2 West deviation makes 096 to steer. Coming back up, the signs flip. So compass 250 minus 2 West is 248 magnetic, minus 4 West is 244 true. Error west, compass best. Error east, compass least. So a westerly error makes the compass read higher. Steer the compass number at the helm, plot the true number on the chart, and if this helped it click, follow for more.
20260724_7662161761583353110.summary: Learners will understand how to use the TVMDC rule to convert between true, magnetic, and compass courses by applying variation and deviation.

20260725_7662162420458212630.description: There is a whole slice of the sea your sailboat physically cannot sail into. In 72 seconds you will learn every point of sail, from the no go zone and close hauled to beam reach, run, and why port tack gives way to starboard. Save this one for your next time on the water. #navigation #boating #seamanship⚓️🚢⛴️ #maritimemaster #learnontiktok #deckcadet #sailing
20260725_7662162420458212630.transcript: There is a whole slice of the sea your sailboat physically cannot sail into. Everything in sailing hangs on one question: where is the wind sitting relative to your bow? About 45 degrees either side of the wind is the no go zone, where the sails just flap and the boat stalls, stuck in irons. Steer just outside that zone, and you are close hauled, sails hauled in tight, clawing your way upwind. Bear away a little more, and you are on a close reach, with the sails eased just a touch. Wind square across the beam and sails about half out is a beam reach, usually your fastest and easiest ride. Keep turning until the wind comes over your back quarter, and you are on a broad reach, sails eased well out. Dead downwind is a run, sails right out, but watch that boom because an accidental gybe can slam it across the deck hard. Whichever side the wind blows over names your tack, and a boat on port tack gives way to a boat on starboard tack. Where the wind sits on your bow decides your sail set and your steering, so learn this dial before you next cast off.
20260725_7662162420458212630.summary: Learners will understand the main points of sail relative to wind direction, from the no-go zone up to a run, as well as basic port and starboard tack give-way rules.

20260726_7664263375391706390.description: A crewmate hits the water and you have minutes, not hours, to get them back. This 72 second drill walks through the first actions that save lives: shout and point, throw the lifebuoy, press MOB, send the Mayday, then a slow approach into the wind with the engine in neutral alongside. Save it and practise the drill with your crew before the day you need it. #manoverboard #maritimetraining #learnontiktok #maritimemaster #deckcadet #boating #navigation #sailing #seafarer⚓️
20260726_7664263375391706390.transcript: One second they are on deck, the next they are in the water, and what you do in the first minute decides whether they come back. Shout man overboard so everyone hears it, and make one person a spotter who points at the casualty and never looks away. A head in waves is a target about the size of a football, so if that pointing finger drops, you may never see them again. Throw the lifebuoy straight away because it gives them something to hold and marks the spot from a distance. Press the MOB button on the GPS or chartplotter so the boat records where they went in. Press the distress button to send the alert, then make a voice Mayday on channel 16, because a person in the water counts as grave and imminent danger, and only cancel it when help is no longer needed, not the moment they are back aboard. Bring the boat round in a controlled turn, not a panic turn, slowing early and keeping the casualty in sight all the way. Under sail, start the engine and check no ropes are trailing before you go into gear. And under power, simply take the speed off early. Motor the final approach into the wind or into wind and sea, slowed right down so you stop beside them, not on top of them. The moment you are alongside, put the engine in neutral or switch it off completely, so the propeller is not turning anywhere near them. Shout and point, throw, press MOB, send the Mayday, come back slow into the wind and go to neutral. Then save this and practice the drill with your crew before the day you need it.
20260726_7664263375391706390.summary: Covers the essential sequence of actions required during a man-overboard emergency, from alarm and Mayday transmission to final approach into the wind.
